concepts.name: Origins and Triggers of the Telangana Uprising (1946–51)
key_dimensions: Role of Nizam's feudal autocracy and the Razakars as immediate catalysts
Distinction between agrarian grievances (vetti, forced labor) and political oppression under Hyderabad State
Why Telangana (not coastal Andhra) became the epicenter — specific socio-economic conditions
UPSC trap: Differentiating the 1946 Telangana uprising from the 1948 Police Action (Operation Polo) — overlapping timelines but distinct causes

concepts.name: Role of the Nizam's Feudal System: Deshmukhs, Doras, and Vetti
key_dimensions: Vetti (forced unpaid labor) as a structural exploitative mechanism specific to Hyderabad State
Doras and Deshmukhs as intermediary landlord classes — distinction from zamindars in British India
How the absence of Permanent Settlement created a different but equally oppressive agrarian structure
UPSC trap: Comparing Hyderabad's jagirdari system with Ryotwari and Zamindari systems — overlaps and unique features

concepts.name: Role of the Communist Party of India (CPI) in the Uprising
key_dimensions: CPI's organizational role through the Andhra Mahasabha — transformation from cultural to revolutionary body
Debate within CPI: 'Peoples War' line (1942) vs. post-war agrarian mobilization strategy
CPI's tactical use of guerrilla warfare — formation of dalam (armed squads)
UPSC trap: CPI's ambiguous stance — simultaneously leading the uprising while navigating the question of supporting/opposing Hyderabad's merger with India

concepts.name: Andhra Mahasabha: Evolution from Cultural to Revolutionary Organization
key_dimensions: Founded 1930 — original mandate of Telugu cultural and educational upliftment
Radicalization under communist leadership (Ravi Narayan Reddy, Baddam Ella Reddy)
How the Mahasabha served as a mass front organization for CPI mobilization
UPSC trap: Andhra Mahasabha's role in Telangana uprising vs. its later role in the Andhra State agitation — same organization, different objectives

concepts.name: Land Redistribution and Agrarian Reforms Achieved During the Uprising
key_dimensions: Approximately 10 lakh acres of land redistributed to landless peasants in liberated zones
Cancellation of usurious debts and abolition of vetti in controlled territories
Formation of village-level guerrilla governments (gram rajyams) — a proto-state structure
UPSC trap: These reforms were extralegal/revolutionary — contrast with later legal land reforms under the Indian Constitution

concepts.name: Razakars and Their Role as a Trigger for Peasant Radicalization
key_dimensions: Razakars as the private militia of Majlis-e-Ittehadul Muslimeen (MIM) under Qasim Razvi
Razakar atrocities against peasants, especially lower castes and communists, intensifying the uprising
Distinction: Razakars represented communal-feudal oppression vs. the class-based peasant resistance
UPSC trap: Razakars are often associated only with anti-merger politics — their direct role in agrarian terror is a less-tested but high-yield angle

concepts.name: Liberated Zones (Guerrilla Squares) and Parallel Governance
key_dimensions: Nalgonda, Warangal, and Khammam districts as the core 'liberated' areas
Establishment of gram rajyams with people's courts (jan adalats) dispensing local justice
Functions performed: land redistribution, debt cancellation, resolution of disputes — a state-within-a-state
UPSC trap: Comparing Telangana's liberated zones with Tebhaga and Punnapra-Vayalar movements — Telangana uniquely achieved proto-governmental structures

concepts.name: Operation Polo (1948) and Its Impact on the Uprising
key_dimensions: Indian military action (September 1948) merged Hyderabad into India — removed the Nizam but not the landlord class
Post-merger paradox: Indian Army deployed against the same peasants it 'liberated' from Nizam
Sardar Patel's directive to suppress the communist uprising after merger — shift from national liberation to class conflict framing
UPSC trap: Operation Polo ended Nizam's rule but NOT the Telangana uprising — the peasant movement continued until 1951

concepts.name: Indian State's Repression of the Uprising (1948–51)
key_dimensions: Use of the Armed Forces (Special Powers) type operations and mass arrests under Hyderabad's Emergency laws
Ravi Narayan Reddy's arrest and the decimation of CPI's ground leadership
Approximately 4,000 peasants/activists killed and 10,000 arrested during the suppression phase
UPSC trap: The Indian government's suppression is often glossed over — the state that conducted Operation Polo against the Nizam simultaneously suppressed the peasant uprising

concepts.name: CPI's Withdrawal from Armed Struggle and the 1951 General Elections
key_dimensions: Andhra Thesis (1951) — P. Sundarayya's strategic document recommending shift to parliamentary path
Comintern/Soviet influence: Moscow's 'peaceful transition' line influenced CPI to contest elections
CPI's electoral success in 1952 in Telangana — validation of mass base built during uprising
UPSC trap: The withdrawal was NOT due to military defeat alone — ideological shift toward parliamentary democracy was equally critical

concepts.name: Key Leaders of the Telangana Uprising: Ravi Narayan Reddy, P. Sundarayya, and Others
key_dimensions: Ravi Narayan Reddy — elected to Constituent Assembly while leading the uprising (unique dual role)
P. Sundarayya — military strategist of the dalam system and later author of the Andhra Thesis
Baddam Ella Reddy and the role of local organizers vs. central CPI leadership
UPSC trap: Ravi Narayan Reddy being a Constituent Assembly member while leading an armed uprising against the Indian state — a constitutional and political paradox

concepts.name: Caste Dimensions of the Telangana Uprising
key_dimensions: Predominantly Kamma and Reddy landlords vs. Madigas, Malas (Scheduled Castes) as primary peasant participants
Uprising challenged both class exploitation (economic) and caste-based vetti (social)
Limits of the CPI's class framework in addressing caste — internal tensions within the movement
UPSC trap: Telangana uprising is often analyzed purely through a class lens — caste as an equally significant dimension is a higher-order analytical question

concepts.name: Comparison with Contemporary Peasant Movements: Tebhaga and Punnapra-Vayalar
key_dimensions: Tebhaga (Bengal, 1946–47): Share-cropping demand (2/3 share) vs. Telangana's land redistribution — different demands
Punnapra-Vayalar (Travancore, 1946): Urban labor + agrarian combination vs. Telangana's purely agrarian base
Telangana uniquely combined: armed struggle + liberated zones + proto-governance — most radical of the three
UPSC trap: All three are CPI-led, contemporaneous, and suppressed — examiner may test the specific distinguishing feature of each

concepts.name: Hyderabad State Congress vs. CPI: Competing Anti-Nizam Nationalisms
key_dimensions: Hyderabad State Congress (HSC) sought merger with India through constitutional means — aligned with INC
CPI sought agrarian revolution first, then merger — or an independent people's republic
HSC's alliance with Indian state post-merger vs. CPI's continued armed resistance — divergence after 1948
UPSC trap: Both HSC and CPI opposed the Nizam, but had fundamentally different post-merger visions — a nuanced comparison question

concepts.name: Legacy of the Telangana Uprising on Land Reforms in Independent India
key_dimensions: Uprising created political pressure for the Hyderabad Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1950
Influenced First Five Year Plan's emphasis on land reforms — Kumarappa Committee's recommendations
CPI's electoral success in 1952 in Andhra forced Congress to accelerate zamindari abolition
UPSC trap: Connecting the Telangana uprising to constitutional provisions — Article 31A (zamindari abolition protection) was partly a response to pressures from such movements

concepts.name: Women's Participation in the Telangana Uprising
key_dimensions: Women's role in intelligence networks, supply chains, and as dalam (squad) members
Andhra Mahasabha's women's wing mobilization — connecting social reform (widow remarriage, literacy) to agrarian struggle
Specific women leaders: Chakali Ilamma — her resistance to landlord Visnur Ramachandra Reddy became iconic
UPSC trap: Chakali Ilamma's story is a high-yield case study — her land was confiscated by a landlord, triggering local revolt; often tested for Mains illustrative examples

concepts.name: Chakali Ilamma: Symbol of Peasant Resistance
key_dimensions: A Dalit washerwoman whose land was seized by Dora Visnur Ramachandra Reddy — sparking organized resistance
Her case exemplifies the intersection of caste, gender, and class oppression in the Telangana context
CPI organized around her case to demonstrate the concrete injustice of the feudal system
UPSC trap: Her story is simultaneously a women's history, Dalit history, and agrarian history question — examiners test which dimension is being asked

concepts.name: Telangana Uprising and the Debate on 'People's Democratic Revolution' within CPI
key_dimensions: Telangana became the test case for CPI's strategic debate: armed revolution vs. parliamentary path
'Zhdanov Thesis' (two-camp theory) and its influence on CPI's decision to intensify armed struggle post-1948
B.T. Ranadive's 'left adventurist' line vs. P. Sundarayya's Andhra Thesis — internal CPI contradiction
UPSC trap: The CPI split of 1964 (CPI vs. CPI-M) has roots in these strategic disagreements first surfaced during Telangana — a long-arc causation question

concepts.name: Telangana Uprising's Influence on Later Naxalite Movements
key_dimensions: Telangana's guerrilla zone model directly inspired the Naxalbari uprising (1967) and Srikakulam (1967–70)
Dalam (squad) system and jan adalat concepts were revived by CPI (ML) in later decades
The unresolved agrarian question in Telangana region contributed to continued Maoist presence in Andhra/Telangana
UPSC trap: Naxalism is a contemporary internal security issue — connecting its ideological roots to the Telangana uprising (Modern History) is a cross-paper, integrative question

concepts.name: Significance of Telangana Uprising in the Context of Indian State Formation
key_dimensions: Demonstrated that integrating princely states required addressing agrarian issues, not just political-military merger
Challenged Nehru-Patel consensus that Operation Polo 'solved' the Hyderabad problem
Contributed to debates on federalism and linguistic reorganization — Andhra State (1953) partly a response to political pressures from the region
UPSC trap: The uprising's contribution to the States Reorganisation Act (1956) is indirect but examinable — Telangana's political awakening fed into the demand for Andhra Pradesh formation
